newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Jardine Matheson pledges commitment to HK, China.
newsitem.headline: Jardine Matheson pledges commitment to HK, China.

text.p: Colonial trading giant Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd, once labelled by Beijing as "the black sheep of business", pledged its commitment to Hong Kong and China during talks with Chinese leaders on Wednesday.

Chairman Henry Keswick and other senior Jardine officials, including managing director Alasdair Morrison, met Chinese Vice-Premier Zhu Rongji and the top Chinese official for Hong Kong, Lu Ping, in Beijing.
"He (Zhu) welcomed our range of activities and numerous joint ventures in China," Keswick said in a statement.
"His interest in the development of our Hong Kong businesses, in a number of which we have partners from the mainland, was both positive and encouraging," he said.
Keswick said Lu also welcomed the development of Jardine's business in Hong Kong and China.
"I stressed the Jardine Matheson Group's commitment to expanding its activities in Hong Kong as well as in mainland China over the long term," he said.

"It is a mark of confidence in the future Special Administrative Region (SAR) and the concept of 'one country, two systems' that multinational companies like Jardines continue to expand their operations here," he added.

China has promised Hong Kong it can continue its free-wheeling capitalist system independent after the British colony reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 to become a Special Administrative Region of China.

The Jardine Group, a major colonial trading house whose history in Hong Kong dates back to its early opium trading days, was once been singled out for a stinging verbal attack by Beijing when it called the firm "the black sheep of business".

Jardines angered Beijing when it shifted its domicile from Hong Kong to Bermuda in 1984. The move came when the ink had barely dried on the Sino-British Joint Declaration, signed that year, governing the return of Hong Kong to Chinese rule.

The delisting of the group's companies from the Hong Kong stock exchange in 1994 and 1995 was viewed by China as a case of rats deserting a sinking ship, although the Jardines board clearly stated its disagreement with Hong Kong's stock market listing regulations was the sole reason for the departure.
Beijing had also objected to a contract awarded to a consortium led by Jardines to develop the territory's ninth container terminal. China eventually approved the project last September.
Keswick said the number of group employees in Hong Kong had doubled to 60,000 since 1984 and that Jardines was the largest private employer in the future SAR.
"Our Group believes in Hong Kong's prosperity and stability after China resumes the exercise of sovereignty," he added.
Jardines was present in 30 Chinese cities and was a partner in 70 joint ventures employing 15,000 people, the statement said.
